# Design and Development of an Automated Gymnastics Movement Evaluation Device.docx (.docx)

Design and Development of an Automated 
Gymnastics Movement Evaluation Device
Ari Bawono Putranto1,a)*, Naurah Elfrida Anargya2,a) Ahmad Ridlo Hanifudin Tahier3,a), Fakhruddin Mangkusasmito4,b, 
aAutomation Engineering Technology, Diponegoro University, Semarang, Indonesia
bIndustrial Electrical Engineering, Diponegoro University, Semarang, Indonesia
Accepted on mmmmm dd, yyyy
Approved on mmmmm dd, yyyy
Abstract— Rhythmic gymnastics need precision, balance, and harmonious body coordination. This study designs an automated rhythmic-gymnastics movement evaluation device based on wearable inertial and orientation sensing. An ADXL335 accelerometer sensor and an HMC5883L magnetometer sensor are integrated with an ESP32-C3 mini transmitter to acquire three-axis acceleration and heading data in real time and stream them via Wi-Fi (UDP) to a Wemos D1 Mini ESP32 as a receiver. The receiver sends data to a PC application that performs downsampling with average pooling to reduce signal density, applies min–max normalisation to harmonise scale across axes, and compares the processed test sequence against reference data. Deviations are quantified through per-parameter error computation, which is converted to accuracy and combined using predefined weights to generate an overall performance score that is displayed on an LCD/P10 panel. Experimental trials on SKJ 2012 warm-up movements show that sequences closely matching the reference pattern consistently yield high scores about 80–85, whereas intentionally incorrect executions produce substantially lower scores around 40. The proposed system therefore provides an objective, repeatable, and real-time scoring mechanism that can support teachers in evaluating movement conformity, reduce assessor bias, and enable measurable feedback for learning and training in school-based physical education.
Keywords:  Rhythmic Gymnastics; ADXL335 Accelerome

arguments.title: Introduction
arguments.content:
Rhythmic gymnastics is a sport that requires precise movements, harmonious body coordination, and consistent timing. The primary objective of gymnastics in the educational context is to improve physical fitness, motor skills, and discipline [1][2]. The intensity of gymnastic movements varies according to the rhythm of the selected music, making each routine distinct in its execution pattern [3][4]. In formal school settings, gymnastics—particularly standardised routines such as SKJ (Senam Kesegaran Jasmani)—serves as a mandatory physical education activity whose learning outcomes must be objectively assessed.

The evaluation of students' gymnastics performance is predominantly conducted through direct visual observation by physical education teachers. In a typical class of 30–40 students performing simultaneously, a single assessor must track multiple individuals, each executing a sequence of coordinated movements. This manual approach introduces several well-documented challenges: (i) assessor fatigue degrades consistency over repeated observations, (ii) subjective interpretation of movement quality varies between assessors and across sessions, (iii) the human eye cannot reliably quantify subtle kinematic deviations such as limb angle errors or timing discrepancies, and (iv) environmental factors—lighting, viewing angle, and occlusions—further compromise accuracy [5]. Consequently, the assessment outcome often reflects the assessor's personal impression rather than the student's actual motor competency. Efforts to mitigate this subjectivity through statistical analysis of inter-rater reliability have been proposed [6]; however, these approaches only detect bias post hoc rather than preventing it at the source.

The research gap lies in the absence of a low-cost, wearable, and real-time automated scoring system specifically designed for structured gymnastics routines in school physical education. While prior work has demonstrated that inertial and magnetic sensors can track human motion, existing implementations suffer from three key limitations. First, studies combining accelerometer and magnetometer sensors with Android applications have achieved only movement monitoring without an automatic scoring mechanism [7]. Second, research employing the HMC5883L magnetometer sensor for shooting practice [8] and accelerometer-gyroscope systems for sit-up monitoring [9] confirms that sensor fusion improves phase detection accuracy, yet these systems were designed for single-plane, repetitive exercises rather than multi-joint, choreographed gymnastics sequences. Third, no prior system has integrated downsampling with average pooling and min-max normalization into a unified pipeline that simultaneously reduces signal density, harmonizes multi-axis data, and maps deviations to a human-interpretable score.

To address this gap, the present study develops an automated gymnastics movement evaluation device with the following scope: (i) the device targets standardized warm-up routines (SKJ 2012) performed by individual students in a controlled indoor environment; (ii) it employs wearable ADXL335 accelerometer and HMC5883L magnetometer sensors transmitting via ESP32-C3 Mini over Wi-Fi (UDP); (iii) the receiver—a Wemos D1 Mini ESP32—forwards raw sensor streams to a PC application that executes downsampling via average pooling, min-max normalization, per-parameter error computation against reference data, and weighted scoring; and (iv) the final score is displayed on an LCD/P10 panel for immediate feedback. The research questions guiding this work are: (RQ1) How can raw three-axis inertial and magnetic sensor data be processed into a normalized sequence suitable for comparison against a reference? (RQ2) How can per-parameter deviations be weighted to produce a final score that correlates with human expert judgment? (RQ3) Does the system differentiate between correct and intentionally incorrect executions with statistically meaningful score separation?

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II describes the system design—covering hardware, communication protocol, and the signal-processing pipeline. Section III details the experimental setup, including participant recruitment, movement protocols, and reference-data collection. Section IV presents the scoring results and analyzes the relationship between motion fidelity and computed scores. Section V concludes with implications for physical education assessment and directions for future work.
